query: What does the author mean by the two rivers running through us?
ideal_answer: The author says two rivers run through us at all times. The first river carries all the voices of the world, and it is strong, steady, and constant with its instruction, guidance, and forewarning. The second river is a single voice that stands alone, which is the voice of our inner guide. Most of us live mindlessly, being pulled toward each milestone we were told to reach for, until we look down and realize our hands are empty. The author says the journey is not about abandoning one river in favor of the other. The journey is about knowing when it is time to listen to, hear, and follow each of them. Our lives begin the day we choose to follow our inner knowing, even while still hearing, and at times heeding, the collective knowledge of the first river.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: What does real happiness actually look like according to the author?
ideal_answer: According to the author, happiness is not what your house looks like but how you love the people within its walls. Happiness is not finding success by a certain time but finding something you love so much that time itself seems to disappear. Happiness is not thinking you have earned the world's approval but waking up each day at peace within your own skin, unconcerned with how you are perceived. Happiness is not having the best of everything but having the ability to make the best of anything. Happiness is knowing you are doing what you can with what you were given.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: How can I stop reacting to everything so quickly? What does the book suggest?
ideal_answer: The author describes self-protection as learning to take a pause between what you feel and how you react. When there is no awareness between what you perceive and the way you respond, anything can control you. The author advises you to practice the pause and widen the space between what you sense and what you do about it. You should decide what is worth your energy, because what you engage with is what you empower.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: What should I do with heavy feelings instead of trying to fix them?
ideal_answer: The author says heavy feelings are not asking for your intervention but for your attention. When you come into full awareness of what you feel, the feeling will gradually release itself. You participate in your own suffering when you delay, avoid, resist, or fracture your awareness of the feeling. When you start noticing the sensations in your body you will probably feel reactive and want to fix, change, or distract yourself from the feeling. Fixing or distracting does not work because the feeling is in you and not in the things you are fixing or changing. The feeling only asks to be metabolized and processed, and eventually it turns into an unconscious wisdom that guides you forward.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Why is it so hard to end suffering, according to the author?
ideal_answer: The author says it is painful to end your suffering because it is painful to process, to feel, to let go, to grieve, to be honest, and to move on. The pain of facing fears is acute but temporary. It is so painful that most people keep themselves in a prolonged state of mild discomfort to avoid that sensation. The author says ending suffering is painful only at first, and that there is peace on the other side and a new life waiting to begin.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Why do I keep repeating the same patterns even when I want to change?
ideal_answer: The author says your brain works against you in ways you do not realize. The compulsion to repeat makes familiar discomfort feel desirable. The negative is disproportionately focused on because it feels like a clearer potential threat. We are evolving beings trying to operate with pieces of a machine developed for the most blunt kind of survival. Growth comes from witnessing those impulses and choosing otherwise again and again until the new choice becomes instinctive and rewired. When you live from what is immediately comfortable, you miss out on what exists beyond where the limits appear to be.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Can I think my way out of fear?
ideal_answer: The author says you cannot think your way out of fear because fear is an irrational force. You will have to leap with your heart racing, again and again, until you have carved out a new comfort zone in the arena of your deepest desires. You will have to learn to live with the invisible thing within you that wants to shield you from anything unknown. You will have to learn to speak to it and comfort it, but above all to defy it. You keep doing this until you have built a new home within you.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: How do I find my purpose in life? Is it something I have to discover?
ideal_answer: The author says your purpose is not a mystery you have to unlock or decode. Your purpose is something you choose from the elements of your passions, your wants, and your inspirations. Your purpose does not come to you out of the blue one day. It is something you pull out from deep inside and make your everyday life.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: How can I grow if I am not yet where I want to be in life?
ideal_answer: The author advises you to go find the souls who are standing on your desired horizon. You should surround yourself with people you admire, people you trust, and people you would want to grow to be. Much of your development happens by osmosis, which is an unconscious acquisition of the traits and thought patterns of those around you. The author says that surrounding yourself with those who are already where you want to be will light your path.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: How do I heal when I can't remove myself from what is causing me pain?
ideal_answer: The author says you heal by learning boundaries. None of us can fully insulate ourselves from the ache of the world, from other broken hearts, or from inevitable stress. The journey was never about that and is only about strengthening yourself from the inside out. You train your mind to be more conscious of what it entertains and act out of true choice, self-preservation, and self-love instead of compulsion or obligation. You look inward at the pieces of yourself you see in the people who bother you most, and you work on healing those pieces. You get better at communicating what you need and you make the changes that need to occur within your own life. You then notice that the situation has not lightened but you have, because you have changed what moment you meet.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: How do I know when to take control of things and when to let go?
ideal_answer: The author says that in an unawakened state your power is fully externalized and you place your faith in systems and structures that never intended to move you past where you are. When you reach exhaustion with that view, you go inward and discover the power within you. As you wake up to that power you often overuse it and assume the universe will bend around you. You shake off that illusion when the things you created do not turn out as perfectly as you imagined and you start taking other people's timing and needs into account. The true journey of your life then becomes the dance between what is yours to handle and what is yours to release. It means knowing when to speak and when to listen, when to teach and when to learn, and when to exert your will and when to surrender. The author calls this understanding your free will and developing the discernment to use it well.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Why does nothing feel right at the beginning, and how can I tell if something is truly right for me?
ideal_answer: The author says nothing feels completely right at the beginning because nothing is completely familiar at the beginning. Your sense of comfort and correctness tends to be rooted in familiarity. The real question is not whether something instantly makes you feel fated for it but whether it grows with you. The right thing gives you the opportunity to stretch, change, and become better. The author says the true test of what is right is not what instantly falls into place but what entwines its roots with yours and lets you blossom. It is also what stays and remains through everything.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Where should I put my energy in life?
ideal_answer: The author says that eventually you have to stop pouring yourself into things that give nothing back and that take without any intent to give. You also have to stop trying to fit into places you are no longer meant to be. If you are going to give your energy to anything, give it to what is already working. That means the people who already love you, the things that show potential, and the places that make you feel more alive. The author says life speaks in subtle ways such as little clicks and funny coincidences, and that the quiet whispers are often the most accurate. The louder voices of pride, ego, and attraction often lack the fullness of truth, so you should listen for the quiet yes.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Is it okay to outgrow things I love?
ideal_answer: The author says you will have to learn to outgrow some things you love. Some things are right for a time but not forever. Moving on from them does not diminish the place they held in you or the impact they had on you. The author says that if you are not growing you are not really living, and that if you are not moving on from anything you are not moving toward something. Letting go of things that are still beautiful is sometimes necessary because you know they are not quite right and a deeper peace is waiting. The author says letting go is not a failure but a signal of completion and one of the truest signs you are evolving.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: What should I do when I don't know what to do next in life?
ideal_answer: The author says that when you do not know what to do next, the next step is usually not far away but right in front of your feet. You are being asked to stop gazing outward and start looking inward. You do not need more answers but need to accept the ones you have already been given. The author says it is time to learn to be in the answered prayer that is this very day and to use what you already have. You should stop waiting for some future scenario to bring your dreams to light. Instead you should dig your dreams out from beneath your fear and truly begin.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Is it wrong to need rest when I feel like I should be productive?
ideal_answer: The author says that on days when it hurts too much to dream or hope, you should just rest. You were raised in a world that believes productivity can only be measured outwardly and that only things others can consume are worth doing. The author says your soul cannot be fooled by this belief. Eventually you give way to your inner being, which knows how vital it is to recover, reintegrate, reflect, and balance all doing with the simplicity of being. The author says there is nothing wrong with you for needing to take life at your own pace. Your unwillingness to press forward in outdated ways is not noncompliance but a sign that the spiritual freedom you have cultivated is beginning to take root.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Are my personality traits fixed, or can my environment change how I am?
ideal_answer: The author suggests you consider that your qualities may not be fixed. Your environment and the structure of your day evoke different emotional states. With consistency, those states can start to look like unmovable aspects of who you are. The author asks what is happening around you when you are your most peaceful, open-minded, and inspired self, and what is happening when you are not. The author raises the possibility that healing could be as simple as making the smallest amendments and seeing how widely their effects ripple.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Should I give up on love?
ideal_answer: The author says there are many things you can give up on, but love is not one of them. You have to believe in real, true, honest love until the very end. Not giving up on love means being open to how and when it may come, and accepting that its deepest form may not look as you pictured. The author says love does not sweep you off your path but helps you stand more firmly on your own two feet. Love does not idealize an idea of you while failing to support the person you are becoming. Love cares for you in constant, simple, human ways. The author says love is not something you find one day but something you learn to see around you and heal yourself into being able to receive.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: What questions should I ask myself before making a big decision?
ideal_answer: The author says that in everything you choose you should first ask what it will do to your soul. You should ask whether it brings you closer to a heavenly state of being or anchors you in the ache of the world. You should ask whether it makes you more of the person you were meant to be or distracts you from the true work. You should ask whether it pays the bills but bankrupts your being, or impresses others but disappoints the child inside you. You should ask whether you will arrive at the end of your life proud that you did it. You should also ask whether you will do it now or wait until you are forced to make the decision you already know is right, and whether you will have courage.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: What is the 'pivot period' the book talks about?
ideal_answer: The author says the space between no longer and not yet defines the pivot periods of our lives. It is a time when we have nothing left to hold onto but also nowhere clearly to land. The author says this is when most people revert to their oldest and most familiar coping mechanisms, confusing what is known with what is right. If we find the courage to keep our hearts open through this process, we create an opportunity for miracles to find us and change us. If we make peace with the unknown and do not require every answer to keep moving, we begin to live more completely in the moment.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Is romantic love the answer to everything? What does the author think?
ideal_answer: The author says that if your heart is healing you should remember there is more to life than romantic love, and there are equal joys and other worthwhile pursuits. The author suggests society may hinge on you believing that marriage and reproduction are the highest thing worth living for. Romantic love does not excuse you from inner work and does not solve every problem, and rushing to find it often complicates our hearts. The pressure to be in a relationship can bend your sense of self until connection feels futile. The author says believing romantic love will sanitize your pain is untrue and unhelpful, because it places the source of your inner peace in someone else's commitment. Our fantasies about other people mirror our unawakened love back to us and remind us to nurture the heart we already have.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: How do I deal with intrusive thoughts that pull me off my path?
ideal_answer: The author says you may have thoughts throughout the day that are intrusive, sudden, and consuming, and that they can always exist in some form. Your job is to notice them before they convince you they are true or a compelling guide. You should ask yourself where the thought intends to bring you and whether it is trying to give deeper clarity or disturb calm waters. You should ask whether it is something your most empathetic, compassionate, and empowered self would believe. You should also ask yourself whether you must act on it and whether you will.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: What makes a life well lived according to the author?
ideal_answer: The author says the measure of a well-lived life is not how often you avoided discomfort, pressure, or change but the grace with which you navigated it. The author says having faced no resistance proves only that you were defined by nothing and tried for nothing. The author says that being disapproved of is not the worst thing in the world. The actual worst thing is paralyzing yourself in an attempt to avoid any friction. What matters is not whether you have faced challenges but the courage with which you faced them, and that is what defines who you are.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: How should I love someone when our connection is fading?
ideal_answer: The author says that when a connection is waning you must remind yourself not to steer another person's destiny. You cannot assume the dream you had for them is the one they have for themselves. To love someone is to allow them to be sovereign and to honor their path and their ability to choose how to spend their life. The author says loving this way is the only way to experience true intimacy. That intimacy is not based on expectation or need but on the free will of two souls who see no better way to spend their energy than on each other. The author says what you are really waiting for is love that is intuitive and clear, that does not make you doubt your worth, and that chooses you as you choose it.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Why don't other people understand my journey?
ideal_answer: The author says not everyone will understand your journey because not everyone is meant to. Not everyone has made peace with their inner longings or paused to reflect on themselves. The nature of your journey can emphasize some people's stuckness, the fortress they feel is an essential shield. The author says someone else's development is unnerving because it reflects the part of us that desires the same change and the part that resists it equally. Your experience is not validated in proportion to how much sense it makes to others. The author says that even if you are the only person who knows where you are going, that is more than enough to get all the way there.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Do I have to share everything about myself with the people around me?
ideal_answer: The author says your story is not for everyone. If people have not proven they intend to hear and hold you gently, you are under no obligation to share the rawest details of yourself. There are some things you are allowed to keep sacred and small. The author says this is not denying yourself but protecting yourself. In a world where it has become normal to broadcast every detail of your existence, it is okay to practice discernment. It is okay to be intentional about who holds your most vulnerable pieces.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: How do you become brave?
ideal_answer: The author says nobody is brave at the beginning and that bravery is dug out of the deepest part of us, often by necessity. It is when your love for something grows a little larger than your fear about it. It is when the voice of possibility becomes a little louder than the voice of doubt. It is feeling hesitation and choosing to act anyway, moving in the right direction one step at a time. The author says nobody gets to the end of life with their heart entirely unscarred, because that would mean they were untouched. You become brave when you realize you do not have to feel calm and certain but only find the strength to keep showing up.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: How do I know if someone's love is right for me?
ideal_answer: The author says that if another person's love does not make you feel safe enough to open up, it is not for you. If it does not make you see yourself more kindly, it is not for you. If it does not make you want to live in the ways you always intended, it is not for you. The author says this is not because you are undeserving but because you are completely deserving of someone who makes you happy not only when you are with them but also when you are not.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: How can I stop worrying about everything that might go wrong?
ideal_answer: The author suggests learning to live with a positive curiosity that corrects the constant wondering about what may be going wrong. You can turn your capacity for downward thinking into something that supports your growth. You can consider how you might be pleasantly surprised, how it may be easier than you think, or how a vital lesson might be trying to emerge. The author points out that the worst-case scenario has rarely come to pass. Ruminating on the worst case does not protect you from it. Instead it allows your mind to piece together and filter that particular reality more clearly into form.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Why do I feel so disillusioned with the way society tells us to live?
ideal_answer: The author says the world tells you that working in eight-hour stretches is productivity and that devoting forty years to a lukewarm career is safety. It tells you that surrounding yourself with as many people as possible is connection and that packing your schedule is fullness. It also tells you that losing what makes you feel most alive is responsibility. The author says it is no surprise you feel disillusioned, because society does not cater to the layers and changes a human soul goes through. You will have to create your own universe within that world. The author hopes the waves you create might inspire someone else and that your life can be a lighthouse for other aching hearts.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: How can I tell if something is right for me without overthinking it?
ideal_answer: The author suggests that instead of trying to figure out whether something is definitely right, you should notice what creates resonance or dissonance. You can ask whether it makes your body gently contract or expand. You can ask whether it gives at least as much energy as it takes and whether it intrigues, fascinates, or compels you. You can ask what there is to be found and where walking the path might lead. The author advises paying attention to your body's subtle responses, such as how you lightly open or close to the experience. You should also tally up the smallest coincidences and let yourself be guided in the quietest ways.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Why do I feel envious of certain people, and what should I do with that feeling?
ideal_answer: The author says a big part of finding yourself is discovering the pieces of yourself you first see in other people. People who embody something familiar but out of reach can evoke the heaviness of envy or the lightness of inspiration, and both are trying to guide you to self-realization. What you observe in others is also dormant in you. The tension you feel does not come from someone else occupying what could be yours. It reveals how much you are suppressing that they allow to flow out of themselves. The author says your ego will want to make these people your enemies, but your soul knows they are your teachers in disguise.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Why do things not work out for me right away, even when I know I have a big destiny?
ideal_answer: The author says one characteristic of having a big destiny is that things do not work out for you right away. There are delays and unexpected times of quiet. The plans you had for your life get unraveled and you are asked to conceive of a new vision, one grander than you had the capacity to imagine at first. The author says these rest periods are actually life's way of giving you an opportunity to work on yourself and invest in who you want to be, to heal and to release. The author says these times are not meant only to be tolerated or waited through, but used. They are quiet gifts that lead you to the path you were really meant to be on.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: How can I be a better listener and support the people I love?
ideal_answer: The author says that when it comes to loving other people, they mostly want to be heard and ultimately need to feel seen. Just as witnessing your own feelings transforms them, you can offer that to others by witnessing them. They do not always need you to solve a problem, interject, or give a well-thought-out response. Sometimes all they need is someone to sit quietly with them and listen, even when their words are messy and going in circles. The author says sometimes all anyone really needs is someone who sees.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: How do I tell the difference between fear and intuition?
ideal_answer: The author says that if something feels wrong with your fullest conviction, you should not do it. This holds even if it will disappoint some people, interrupt your trajectory, scare you, or make you question everything you knew. The author says one day you will realize there is a difference between fear and intuition. Fear is something you can reason with, while intuition stands firm. When you find that firmness within you, you should honor it, because it is a guide from deep within.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Why do I care so much about what other people think of me?
ideal_answer: The author says nothing withholds you from your life as much as living in other people's heads. When you unconsciously believe that experiencing love means earning it from others, you construct an image of who you are instead of living the reality of who you might be. You cannot truly control how you are seen, you can only project and assume. What you imagine others see says more about your subconscious psychology than any external perception. The author advises that instead of trying to get others to see you a certain way, you should actually become that way in real time. That is the difference between grazing the surface of life and diving all the way in.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: How does the story I tell myself shape my life?
ideal_answer: The author says you either see endings or new beginnings within them. You either see that you are living the days your younger self dreamed of or you are still waiting for something more. You either see a storm that disrupts your path or one that corrects your course. The author says there is what you experience and then the story you tell yourself about it. Over time that story becomes the truth you carry while other details fade. How you write the narrative determines how you experience reality.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Is being cynical or ironic a healthy way to protect myself?
ideal_answer: The author says an honest heart is rare and that irony and cynicism are shields. They are a way to laugh off your life so it cannot truly touch you. The author says this slowly ices you out of your own experience until you wake up surrounded but lonely and busy but disengaged. If you want a full life you have to be willing to open yourself to it. You have to let it move you, change you, free you, and make you feel again. You should let what is heavy hurt and what is healing lighten, and move through it all without getting too attached.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: How do I figure out what I really want?
ideal_answer: The author says you figure out what you really want by imagining a life that would be too good to be true. Then you take note of its elements and themes. You can ask whether you are surrounded by others or quiet, hopeful or healing or resting, adventuring in the wild, or creating. The picture does not have to fully come true for you to understand that its pieces are directing you to the most honest aspects of yourself. The author then advises you to make a map of that life and live it now, right where you are.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: What if I feel like I'm failing or falling behind in life?
ideal_answer: The author says the parts of your journey where you felt you were failing and falling behind were not setbacks but breakthroughs in disguise. That includes times when nothing worked, when you were forced to rest, when you had to begin self-reflection, and when you had no choice but to change. The author says the universe is constantly asking whether you are ready to stop engaging with old habits and enter a parallel life. You build that life in the gaps between what happens and how you respond. The next time you face the same challenge, you are called to ask how you can respond differently this time.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: How do I keep going when I'm afraid of the future?
ideal_answer: The author asks you to remember the mountains you have scaled before and the nights you were convinced you would never move beyond where you were. Then something small brought you a little ease, and then a little more. You let the waves of big feelings crash over you and then recede. You found courage, softness, forms of love you never expected, and you began to feel enough because you decided what would be enough for you. You developed resilience and discovered your strength is limitless. The author says the things you do now were once the things you prayed to have. Each time you stepped forward, the road rose to meet you, and the author says it will again.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: How do I attract what is meant for me instead of trying to force it?
ideal_answer: The author says everything changes when you shift from trying to force outcomes to attracting the particular things meant for you. The author compares it to a surrender, like letting a butterfly sit gently on your shoulder and become yours because a force beyond you has bound you together. Your priority becomes being the strongest, clearest, kindest version of yourself and honing the skills that are uniquely yours. Your priority also becomes caring deeply for yourself in sincere ways. When you are nurtured, it changes how you interact with the world and what is attracted to you. The author says the things meant for you are drawn to you when your light is on, so you should focus on turning it on.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Should I keep holding on to my daydreams and big ideas?
ideal_answer: The author says you should not retire your daydreams. Everything that exists began in someone's mind, a mind that first had to believe in its own idea enough to make it real. You might not see your dream in front of you yet, but if you feel it within, you have the capacity to bring it to life. The author says bridging the space between what you envision and what you actually experience is the journey of your life.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: What would change if I knew my time in life was limited?
ideal_answer: The author asks you to imagine there were only sixty more holidays left in your life, or fifty more summers, or ten more sunrises you would wake early enough to watch. The author also asks what if you have already read your favorite book, or only have three more times or even one time left to see someone you love. The author then asks how fast that changes things, to think you may not have forever even though it feels like you have much longer. The author asks how differently you would gaze at sacred, irreplaceable days. The author says you would pay more attention and see more.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: How should I handle people who feel threatened by my growth?
ideal_answer: The author says people who have not learned to see their own envy as a signal of where they are destined to excel will see your growth as a threat. The author's response is to grow anyway. People who have not reconciled their own desire for deep change will see your changes only through fear, and the author says to change anyway. People who have not found their own voices will think yours is too loud, and the author says to speak anyway. People who have not healed their wounds will find your wholeness naive, and the author says to rejoice anyway.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Why am I most afraid of the things I am meant for?
ideal_answer: The author says you are often most afraid of what you are meant for. You fear the unknown even though life is almost nothing but a series of unknowns. You fear change and growth even though you are designed for nothing but that. You are most afraid of love when you want it more than anything, and most afraid of your own greatness when it is pressing to be released. The author says this is why facing your worst fears often leads to your greatest growth. Behind that wall is often what you were searching for all along.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Will I ruin my life if I make the wrong decision?
ideal_answer: The author says fearing a wrong turn assumes life is a fixed set of events that unfold according to one decision made or not made, which is a gross underestimation of what life is. Life is a fluid energy that constantly reorients itself around our moment-to-moment choices. The things you call destined are blueprints embedded within you, and you will land on them because they are within you. You will express your inner truth one way or another, but how it appears on the outside is malleable and changes by the moment. The author says you are a free-willed being on an open-ended planet, and that your soul may set the destination but your brain navigates your course.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Do I need a five-year plan to get somewhere in life?
ideal_answer: The author says that more than a five-year plan, you need a vision for the next hour, the next day, and the next week. If you fill your immediate future with things you know are good and productive for you, you will arrive somewhere worthwhile even if you cannot see beyond the horizon right now. The author says that if you learn to live with integrity in the present, one day you will wake up fully immersed in the peace you have been practicing for a very long time.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Why does trying to prove myself never make me feel worthy?
ideal_answer: The author says the compulsion to prove yourself does not strengthen your sense of self-worth but slowly diminishes it. It leaves you constantly finding one more thing to prove that you are in the right group, have the right things, and are on the right path. The author says it comes from a place that denies beauty and assumes you are not enough. We seek outside affirmation because our first-person experience is numbed by a wall we built around our hearts. The author advises dismantling that wall piece by piece. The more your life is enough for you, the less you will need it to be enough for other people.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be

query: Where does my strength and happiness actually come from?
ideal_answer: The author says your strength, power, and happiness are a force that lives within you. They are not in the last chapter of your life, in another person, or in one specific opportunity coming to be. Your ability to find joy and meaning and to radiate pure love is with you always. The author says the rest is a mind game and an activation process of realizing that everything you were seeking from outside was always waiting within you. The author advises you to offer your own love to your own life and to learn to see as beautifully as you can, saying it will change everything forever.
source: The Pivot Year: 365 Days To Become The Person You Truly Want To Be
